metadata.title: The Data Source, Not the Database.
metadata.subtitle: The Notion API Skill
metadata.purpose: Take the Notion API apart in the Teardown register: does Claude query a database directly, or is there a piece underneath doing the actual work? Lands the carry-out — Claude queries the data source underneath the database, not the database itself, and a missing page is almost always a sharing problem, not a bad ID. Names the design call (split the presentation layer from the table itself) and the trade it forces on every API caller.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: hand Claude a database ID and it queries the database — because that's how every other database on earth works. Notion made a different call. Every database has a data source underneath it, and queries have to hit that instead. Why the split?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. The database is a shell — the real table lives one layer down, in a data source. That's where the schema and every row actually sit; a row itself is just a page whose parent is that data source. So schema reads, queries, and creating a new row all have to be aimed at the data source ID. Hand Notion the database ID by mistake and it tells you the object doesn't exist. The design call: separate what a table is from what a database presents. It buys them multiple views on one source without duplicating rows — and it costs every API caller one extra concept to keep straight. Two bundled scripts do the common work: notion_search.sh walks the workspace and paginates every result; notion_read_page.sh reads a full page block by block, in the order you'd read it.

Two details trip everyone up. First — every request has to carry a specific version header. Leave it off and Notion doesn't even look at what you asked; the call fails immediately with a missing-version error. Second — when a call comes back empty, or says the object wasn't found, that's almost never a bad ID. It almost always means the page hasn't been shared with Claude's connection yet. Notion collapsed 'not authorized' and 'doesn't exist' into the same response — probably for privacy — so you'll spend twenty minutes second-guessing the ID before it occurs to you to check sharing. Check sharing first.

beats.narration_text: A few things are easy to miss. First — the page-reading script lists a nested sub-page or sub-database when it hits one, but it doesn't open it. That's a deliberate stopping rule; recursion blows up on deeply nested workspaces, so the script hands you the reference and lets you decide whether to descend. Second — any file link inside a block, an image included, expires after about an hour. It's a signed URL, not a permanent one; never something to save and reuse. Third — when a result list has more pages, the code pulling them has to watch for an error coming back mid-stream, or the loop can run forever instead of stopping. Fourth — filtering a database isn't one-size-fits-all; the right condition depends on the property's type. Select takes 'equals,' multi-select takes 'contains,' date takes 'before' or 'after.' Reading the schema first isn't optional — it's the only way to know which condition applies to which column.

Here's the whole thing in one sentence. Claude doesn't query the database — it queries the data source one layer underneath, and it needs that ID, not the database's. And when something can't be found, the ID is almost never the problem. It's sharing.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to understand how the Notion API distinguishes a database from a data source, and why the split exists. Walk me through what a client sees when it queries a database ID versus the data source ID underneath, including the exact error each returns. Show me a minimal typed filter for a select, a multi-select, and a date property, and explain what fails silently if I get the property type wrong. Go deeper: ask how you'd redesign the API if you optimized for one-view-per-database — the way every other database on earth works — and what that would cost users who currently point multiple views at a single source. Liam, in for Bear.
